title: Saved!
full_review:
Midway through "Saved!" (United Artists), a tart teen comedy set in the world of a conservative Christian high school, the film's ostracized protagonist picks up a Bible hurled at her back and declares to her predatorily pious peers, "This is not a weapon!"

Directed by Brian Dannelly, the film uses satire to offer a scalding critique of puffed-up piety. But by bashing conservative Christians, the movie winds up displaying the same sort of insensitivity it purportedly decries.

Jena Malone stars as Mary, a docile student at an evangelical high school, whose "perfect Christian boyfriend," Dean (Chad Faust), throws her for a loop when, on the eve of their senior year, he tells her that he thinks he is gay.

After mistaking a long-haired pool cleaner for a mystical vision of Jesus, she vows to do whatever it takes to "straighten" things out, even if it means surrendering her virginity for the cause and sleeping with her boyfriend. Her carnal conversion techniques prove fruitless and she winds up pregnant, sending her into a spiritual tailspin that causes her to question everything she's believed in.

Mandy Moore plays Hilary Faye, Mary's best friend, a self-righteous snit and queen bee of the school's sanctimonious sorority, the "Christian Jewels." In one scene Hilary takes target practice at a shooting range, explaining as she pumps another clip into her chrome-plated firearm that she is going to protect her virginity, "using force if necessary."

Hilary betrays Mary's trust by outing Dean, who has been shipped off by his disgraced parents to a treatment facility called "Mercy House," and by organizing a school prayer group to seek divine intervention in curing Dean of his "spiritually toxic affliction."

Hilary and her holier-than-thou harpies turn on the increasingly apostate Mary, who struggles to keep her pregnancy hidden under baggy sweaters. Deemed a pariah, Mary finds herself alone, until she befriends a pair of fellow outcasts: Roland (Macaulay Culkin), Hilary's wheelchair-bound brother, and the rebellious Cassandra (Eva Amurri), the school's lone Jew.

Martin Donavan plays the school's hip but conscience-conflicted principal, Pastor Skip, who becomes involved with Mary's lonely widowed mom (Mary-Louise Parker). Patrick Fugit provides the film's other romantic interest for Mary as Pastor Skip's heartthrob son -- a competitor on the Christian skateboarding circuit.

Dannelly contends that, despite some exaggerations for comedic effect, "Saved!" is not intended to be anti-Christian, but rather is about love and tolerance -- an argument which, after viewing the film, holds little holy water. Characters who take their beliefs seriously are caricatured, at best, as wishy-washy milksops like Pastor Skip, who views Mary's pregnancy as divine chastisement for his affair with her mother or, at worst, as mean-spirited hypocrites like Hilary.

Of course, "Saved!" exposes its ideological slant by making the irreverent and foul-mouthed Cassandra the film's most truly "Christian" character -- with a close second being Roland, who seems almost bored with his faith. It is as if the movie is trying to say that religious convictions are impediments to compassion and genuine spirituality. And though the film ends on an ambiguously pro-faith note, the spirituality proposed is more of the fluffy-feel-good, nondogmatic brand than a costly grace which places moral demands on the believer.

While the film's mocking tone and unflattering wall-to-wall stereotyping of fundamentalists will leave evangelicals feeling anything but enraptured, much of what passes as humor should leave an equally bad taste in the mouths of mainline Protestants and Catholics as well. Feather-ruffling elements range from garden variety digs at conservative Christians to blatantly insensitive jokes, including a crassly irreverent zinger about the crucifixion during a tacky high-school production of "Jesus Christ Superstar."

But turning the critical cheek, "Saved!" does seem sincere in trying to remind viewers that religion can be twisted into something divisive rather than unifying, and can be used as an excuse for intolerance. The film also deserves credit for showing a young, unwed mother taking responsibility for her actions, rather than opting for the easy abortion route. Ironically, however, Planned Parenthood -- the world's largest abortion provider -- gets special thanks in the end credits.

During the climax, Hilary drives her SUV into a large billboard statue of Jesus, causing his head to crash into her windshield. As she stumbles out and stares at the decapitated Jesus, it seems as if the filmmaker is saying that we must take it upon ourselves to be the face of Christ for each other in our world.
Still, when it comes to "Saved!" the only thing worth saving is your money.

Due to religious stereotypes, an implied teen sexual encounter, homosexual references, recurring rough and crude language, profanity and several blasphemous jokes, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is L -- limited adult audience, films whose problematic content many adults would find troubling. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents are strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
